title: Home Theater Setup Guide: 5 Components, Layout, Calibration
metaDescription: A home theater setup needs 5 components: display, AV receiver, speakers, subwoofer and sources. Dolby placement angles, sub placement and calibration steps.
keywords: best subwoofer placement for home theater
best crossover settings for home theater
best home theater setup for apartment
intro:
The **best home theater setup components** are a display sized for your seating distance, an AV receiver with enough channels and good room correction, matched speakers placed at the angles Dolby recommends, and at least one subwoofer placed where the room lets it perform. This guide walks through choosing a configuration, buying the right parts, placing them, and calibrating the result.

If you want a proven starting point, build around the [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/): seven amplified channels for a 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos layout, Audyssey room correction and HEOS streaming. Pair it with the speakers and subwoofer below, then follow the placement and calibration steps.
quickAnswer: A great home theater setup needs five components: a **display** (TV or projector), an **AV receiver**, **front, center and surround speakers**, a **subwoofer**, and **sources** such as a streamer or 4K Blu-ray player. For most rooms, a **5.1.2 Dolby Atmos** layout is the best value: place fronts at 22 to 30 degrees from center, surrounds at 90 to 110 degrees, and height speakers overhead, then run the receiver's room correction and set crossovers to 80 Hz.

picks.body:
The [Denon](/brands/denon/) AVR-X1800H is the receiver we'd start most systems with. It has **7.2 channels**, which is exactly what a **5.1.2 Atmos** layout needs: five ear-level speakers plus two height speakers, all amplified internally, with outputs for two subwoofers.

Denon rates it at **80 watts per channel into 8 ohms (20 Hz to 20 kHz, 0.08% THD, two channels driven)**. With all channels driven, real output per channel is lower, but paired with reasonably sensitive speakers in a medium room it has plenty of headroom. It includes **Audyssey MultEQ XT** room correction, HEOS multiroom streaming, and HDMI inputs that support 8K and 4K at 120 Hz for current consoles.

The trade-off: seven channels caps you at 5.1.2 or 7.1. If you want 7.1.4 or 5.1.4 later, you need a receiver with more processing and amplification, such as the [Denon AVR-X3800H](/gear/denon-avr-x3800h/), so buy for the layout you will want in a few years. See our [home theater receiver guide](/best-home-theater-receiver/) for alternatives.

[Klipsch](/brands/klipsch/)'s Reference R-625FA 5.1.2 system solves the hardest part of a first Atmos setup: height speakers. Its towers have **built-in up-firing Dolby Atmos drivers**, so you get the ".2" height layer without cutting holes in the ceiling. The package adds an **R-52C center**, two **R-41M** bookshelf surrounds and an **R-100SW** subwoofer with a 10-inch driver and 300 W amplifier, so you have a complete 5.1.2 system with the same tweeter and woofer family, and consistent tonal character, across the main channels.

Klipsch's horn-loaded tweeters make these speakers efficient, so they play loud on modest receiver power, a good match for the X1800H above. Matching the center to the front speakers matters more than most buyers realize: dialogue that pans from left to center to right stays the same voice.

The trade-off: up-firing Atmos depends on your ceiling. It works best with a flat, hard, reflective ceiling at typical residential height; vaulted or acoustically treated ceilings weaken the effect, and in-ceiling speakers will always place sounds more precisely. Klipsch's horn sound is also lively, which some listeners find bright in hard-surfaced rooms, and in rooms much over 2,700 cubic feet the 10-inch sub is the first thing to upgrade; the SB-1000 Pro below is the natural step. Compare options in our [Atmos system guide](/best-dolby-atmos-home-theater-system/).

If one component transforms a home theater, it is a good subwoofer, and the [SVS](/brands/svs/) SB-1000 Pro is the one we'd add to almost any system. It uses a **12-inch driver in a sealed cabinet** driven by a **325-watt RMS amplifier (820 watts peak)**, and SVS rates its response at **20 to 270 Hz (plus or minus 3 dB)**.

Sealed subwoofers trade a little maximum output for tight, accurate bass that blends easily with speakers. That suits small to medium rooms. A 14 by 18-foot room with an 8-foot ceiling is about 2,000 cubic feet, comfortably within the SB-1000 Pro's range at sensible movie volumes. Its smartphone app adjusts crossover, phase, room gain and parametric EQ from the listening seat, which makes integration much easier.

The trade-off: very large or open-plan rooms, or a love of reference-level explosions, call for a larger ported model or two subwoofers. Our [subwoofer guide](/best-subwoofer-for-home-theater/) covers bigger options.

picks.award: Best TV for a Living-Room Theater
picks.body:
If your theater is a living room or a room you cannot fully darken for a projector, the [LG](/brands/lg/) C5 OLED is the display we'd pick. OLED pixels produce their own light and switch off completely, so blacks are true black in dark scenes, and contrast does not depend on room darkness the way a projector's does.

It has **four HDMI 2.1 ports** with 4K at up to 144 Hz for gaming, **eARC** to pass lossless Dolby Atmos to your receiver, and supports Dolby Vision and HDR10. It comes in sizes from 42 inches up to very large screens, so you can size it to your seating distance.

The trade-off is brightness and size per dollar. The C5 is not as bright as LG's G-series or the best Mini LED TVs in very sunny rooms, and above about 85 inches a projector delivers far more screen for the money. See our [TV guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/) or [projector guide](/best-projector-for-home-theater/).

sections.heading: Choose Your Configuration First
sections.body:
Speaker configurations are written as **ear-level speakers . subwoofers . height speakers**. A 5.1.2 system has five ear-level speakers, one subwoofer and two height speakers.

| Layout | Speakers | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | Left, right, subwoofer | Small rooms, music-first setups |
| 3.1 | Adds a center channel | Clear dialogue without surrounds |
| 5.1 | Adds two surrounds | The classic surround setup for most rooms |
| 7.1 | Adds two rear surrounds | Long rooms with seating away from the back wall |
| 5.1.2 | 5.1 plus two height speakers | Best value Dolby Atmos |
| 7.1.4 or 5.1.4 | Four height speakers | Dedicated theaters with the budget and receiver to match |

The best home theater configuration for most living rooms is **5.1 or 5.1.2**. Choose 7.1 only if there are at least a few feet between your seats and the back wall for the rear speakers. Choose four height speakers when you can mount them in the ceiling and your receiver can power or process eleven channels.

sections.heading: Best Home Theater Setup Components Checklist
sections.body:
Use this checklist before you buy:

- **Display:** a TV or projector sized for your seating distance. Use the [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/) and, for projectors, the [projector throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/).
- **AV receiver:** enough amplified channels for your layout, [HDMI 2.1](/glossary/hdmi-2-1/) inputs for 4K120 sources, [eARC](/glossary/earc/), and [room correction](/glossary/room-correction/).
- **Front left and right speakers:** bookshelf or tower speakers matched in brand and series.
- **Center channel:** from the same series as the fronts, so voices sound consistent.
- **Surround speakers:** bookshelf, on-wall or in-wall models.
- **Height speakers (for Atmos):** in-ceiling, on-ceiling or up-firing modules.
- **Subwoofer:** sized for room volume; two subs smooth bass across more seats.
- **Sources:** a 4K streamer and, for the best quality, a 4K Blu-ray player.
- **Infrastructure:** [speaker wire](/best-speaker-wire-for-home-theater/) of the right gauge, HDMI cables, a [surge protector](/best-surge-protector-for-home-theater/) and a [universal remote](/best-universal-remote-for-home-theater/).

sections.heading: How to Split Your Budget
sections.body:
There is no perfect formula, but this split works for most separate-component systems:

| Component | Share of budget |
|---|---|
| Speakers (fronts, center, surrounds, heights) | 35% to 40% |
| Display | 25% to 35% |
| Subwoofer | 10% to 15% |
| AV receiver | 15% to 20% |
| Cables, mounts, power, remote | 5% |

Speakers get the largest share because they shape the sound more than anything else and last through several receivers. For a budget home theater setup under $1,000 including a TV you already own, a [quality soundbar](/best-soundbar-for-home-theater/) or a [budget system](/best-budget-home-theater-system/) usually beats a cheap component system. In the $2,000–$5,000 range, separate components start to pull clearly ahead.

sections.heading: Speaker Placement by Dolby Guidelines
sections.body:
Dolby's home theater guidelines give angles measured from the main seat, with 0 degrees pointing straight at the screen:

| Speaker | Horizontal angle from center | Height |
|---|---|---|
| Center | 0 degrees | As close to ear height as possible, angled toward listeners |
| Front left and right | 22 to 30 degrees | Tweeters near ear height |
| Surround left and right (5.1) | 90 to 110 degrees | Ear height or slightly above |
| Side surrounds (7.1) | 90 to 110 degrees | Ear height or slightly above |
| Rear surrounds (7.1) | 135 to 150 degrees | Ear height or slightly above |

**The maths for front speakers:** if your main seat is 10 feet from the front wall, a 30-degree angle puts each front speaker about 5.8 feet to the side of center (10 x tan 30 degrees), or 11.5 feet apart. At 22 degrees, it is about 4 feet each side, or 8 feet apart. Most living rooms land in between.

Toe the front speakers in slightly toward the main seat, keep them at equal distances from it, and leave space between speakers and side walls where possible.

sections.heading: Height Speakers for Dolby Atmos
sections.body:
For **two height speakers** (5.1.2 or 7.1.2), Dolby recommends placing them overhead, slightly in front of or directly above the main seat, at an elevation of roughly **65 to 100 degrees** when viewed from the seat. For **four height speakers**, place the front pair at about **30 to 55 degrees** of elevation in front of you and the rear pair at about **125 to 150 degrees** behind you, each roughly in line with the front left and right speakers.

**Up-firing (Atmos-enabled) speakers** sit on top of the front speakers or towers and bounce sound off the ceiling. They work best with flat, hard ceilings at typical residential height. They are the easiest option for renters and finished rooms; in-ceiling speakers are more precise. See our [in-ceiling speaker guide](/best-in-wall-speakers-for-home-theater/).

sections.heading: Subwoofer Placement
sections.body:
Room shape controls bass more than the subwoofer does, so placement is worth an hour of effort.

**The subwoofer crawl:** put the subwoofer at your main seat, play bass-heavy content or a test tone, then crawl around the room's front half at floor level. Where the bass sounds strongest and most even, place the subwoofer. Front corners often give the most output, but not always the smoothest response.

**Two subwoofers are better than one.** Research on small rooms has shown that two subs, for example at the midpoints of opposite walls, give more even bass across several seats than one sub anywhere. Your AV receiver can then measure and level them together.

Avoid placing the main seat against the back wall, where bass piles up, or dead-center in the room, where some bass notes cancel. Seats about a third of the room's length from the back wall often sound smoother.

sections.heading: Projector or TV Setup and Viewing Distance
sections.body:
For a cinema-like view, aim for the screen to fill about **30 to 40 degrees** of your field of view. A 65-inch 16:9 TV is about 57 inches wide; at a 36-degree viewing angle, the ideal distance is about 87 inches, or just over 7 feet. A 120-inch projector screen is about 105 inches wide, so the same angle puts the seat about 13.5 feet away. Check your room with the [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

Mount the screen so its center sits slightly above seated eye height. For projectors, use the [throw calculator](/tools/projector-throw-calculator/) to find the mounting distance for your projector's [throw ratio](/glossary/throw-ratio/), and control light: a dark room matters more than extra lumens. On TVs, use Filmmaker Mode or the Cinema preset and turn off motion smoothing.

sections.heading: Connections and Wiring
sections.body:
For the simplest high-quality setup:

- Connect **sources to the AV receiver** by HDMI, and the receiver's HDMI output to the TV or projector. Or connect sources to a TV and send audio back to the receiver over **eARC**, which carries lossless Dolby Atmos.
- Use **Ultra High Speed HDMI** cables for 4K120 and gaming.
- Use the right **speaker wire gauge** for each run, and keep polarity consistent.
- Connect the subwoofer to the receiver's **sub or LFE output** with an RCA cable.
- Plug everything into one surge protector so components share a ground, which also reduces hum.

sections.heading: Calibration Step by Step
sections.body:
Calibration is where a good system becomes a great one, and it costs nothing.

1. **Set the subwoofer** to its LFE input (or set its own crossover to maximum or bypass), phase at 0 and volume knob near the middle.
2. **Run room correction** (Audyssey, YPAO, Dirac Live, MCACC or Sony's DCAC). Put the microphone on a tripod at seated ear height, not on a sofa back, and measure the main seat first, then nearby seats.
3. **Check speaker sizes and crossovers.** Set all speakers to Small with a [crossover](/glossary/crossover/) of **80 Hz**, the THX recommendation and the best default. Use 100 to 120 Hz for small satellites; go lower only for large towers that genuinely play deep.
4. **Check distances and levels.** Room correction usually gets these right. If adjusting by hand, use an SPL meter on C-weighting and set each channel to the same level from the main seat.
5. **Fine-tune bass and dialogue by ear.** Many people prefer the subwoofer 2 to 4 dB above flat for movies, and some raise the center channel 1 to 2 dB for clearer dialogue.
6. **Leave bass and treble controls flat** and let room correction handle EQ. If you must adjust, cut rather than boost.
7. **Test with demo scenes** from our [best movies for home theater guide](/best-movies-for-home-theater/).

mistakes.title: Buying more channels than the room can place
mistakes.body: A 7.1.4 receiver is wasted if rear surrounds have to sit against the seats. Choose the layout the room supports.

mistakes.title: Mismatched front and center speakers
mistakes.body: Different brands or series make voices change tone as they pan across the screen. Match the center to the fronts.

mistakes.title: Setting speakers to Large
mistakes.body: Most speakers are better set to Small with an 80 Hz crossover so the subwoofer handles deep bass.

mistakes.title: Measuring room correction from a sofa back
mistakes.body: Reflections from cushions distort the measurement. Use a tripod at ear height and follow the mic prompts.

mistakes.title: Ignoring the room
mistakes.body: Bare walls and hard floors make any system sound harsh. Our [room design guide](/home-theater-room-design/) covers rugs, curtains and panels.

faqs.q: What is the best home theater setup for most people?
faqs.a: A 5.1.2 Dolby Atmos setup is the best value for most rooms: front left and right, a center channel, two surrounds, a subwoofer and two height or up-firing speakers, run by a seven-channel AV receiver with room correction. It delivers convincing surround and overhead effects without the cost of a 7.1.4 system.

faqs.q: Where should surround speakers be placed?
faqs.a: Following Dolby's guidelines, place 5.1 surrounds at 90 to 110 degrees from the center line, just beside or slightly behind the main seat, at ear height or a little above. In a 7.1 layout, add rear surrounds behind the seats at 135 to 150 degrees.

faqs.q: What is the best crossover setting for home theater?
faqs.a: 80 Hz is the best default crossover for most home theater speakers and is the THX recommendation. Set speakers to Small, use 80 Hz, and let the subwoofer handle everything below. Use a higher crossover, around 100 to 120 Hz, for very small satellite speakers.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to put a subwoofer?
faqs.a: The best spot is where bass sounds smoothest at your main seat, found with the subwoofer crawl: place the sub at your seat, play bass, then listen at floor level around the room. Front corners give the most output. Two subwoofers on opposite walls give more even bass across several seats.

faqs.q: Should I buy a soundbar or a component home theater?
faqs.a: A soundbar is better for small rooms, simple setups and budgets under about $1,000. Component systems with an AV receiver and separate speakers sound fuller, place surround and height effects more convincingly and can be upgraded piece by piece. See our soundbar vs home theater comparison for details.

faqs.q: What is the best home theater setup for an apartment?
faqs.a: In an apartment, use a 5.1 or 5.1.2 system with up-firing height modules instead of ceiling speakers, a sealed subwoofer placed on an isolation pad away from shared walls, and room correction. Keep the subwoofer level modest at night. A good Atmos soundbar with wireless surrounds is the simplest alternative.

faqs.q: Do I need professional home theater calibration?
faqs.a: Most people do not. Modern room correction such as Audyssey, YPAO or Dirac Live gets you most of the way when the mic is placed correctly. Professional calibration helps in dedicated rooms with multiple subwoofers or projectors, where an installer can fine-tune bass integration and picture settings.

bottomLine: The best home theater setup components are a display sized to your seating distance, a receiver like the [Denon AVR-X1800H](/gear/denon-avr-x1800h/), matched speakers such as the [Klipsch R-625FA 5.1.2 system](/gear/klipsch-r-625fa-51-system/), and a subwoofer like the [SVS SB-1000 Pro](/gear/svs-sb-1000-pro/), with the [LG C5 OLED](/gear/lg-c5-oled/) as a strong display for rooms that are not fully dark. Pick the configuration your room supports, place speakers at Dolby's angles, crawl for the best subwoofer spot, and run room correction with an 80 Hz crossover.
